matched.note: Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 Dec 2027 (moved from 2 Aug 2026 by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, fixed date).

matched.title: AI literacy
matched.note: Applies to every provider and deployer. Wording softened by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744; no specific literacy level is required.

matched.title: GDPR: lawful basis, transparency and security
matched.note: GDPR applies alongside the AI Act (AI Act Art. 2(7)). The GDPR changes in the Digital Omnibus proposal COM(2025) 837 are not adopted; this follows the GDPR in force. Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

matched.title: GDPR: AI vendors as processors
matched.note: A provider that uses customer data beyond the customer's instructions becomes a controller for that processing (Art. 28(10)). Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

matched.title: GDPR: data protection impact assessment
matched.note: Conservative: triggered by any AI Act high-risk area, profiling, solely automated significant decisions, or special-category data (Art. 35(3) and the DPC's list of high-risk processing). A FRIA can reuse the DPIA (AI Act Art. 27(4)). Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

matched.title: GDPR: solely automated decisions with significant effects
matched.note: Easiest fix is often real human review of each decision, which takes it out of Art. 22. Special-category data in these decisions needs explicit consent or substantial public interest (Art. 22(4)). Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

obligations.text: Train staff who run or use the AI, and keep a record.
Use it according to the provider's instructions.
Assign trained, competent people to oversee it.
Make sure the input data you control is relevant to the purpose.
Monitor it, and suspend it and tell the provider if it poses a risk.
Keep the logs it generates for at least six months.
Tell people when AI helps make decisions about them.
Explain the decision to an affected person who asks.
If you are a public body or provide a public service, do a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use.
Before using it at work, inform workers' representatives and the affected workers.
Pick and record a lawful basis for using the personal data.
Tell people what data you use, why, for how long, and that AI is involved.
Use only the personal data you need, and keep it no longer than needed.
Let people access, correct and delete their data, and object.
Keep the personal data secure (access control, encryption, logging).
Have a data processing agreement with every AI vendor that handles the personal data for you.
If the data leaves the EEA (e.g. a US model API), use a transfer tool such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or SCCs.
Do a data protection impact assessment before you start, and review it when the system changes.
If high risk remains after mitigation, consult the data protection authority before starting.
Only make these decisions if needed for a contract, allowed by law, or with explicit consent.
Let people get a human to review the decision, give their view and contest it.
Explain the logic involved and the likely consequences to the people affected.

obligations.text: Train staff who run or use the AI, and keep a record.
Tell people they are talking to an AI, from the first message.
Under your own brand, you must show the AI notice yourself.
Mark outputs as AI-generated in a machine-readable way.
Pick and record a lawful basis for using the personal data.
Tell people what data you use, why, for how long, and that AI is involved.
Use only the personal data you need, and keep it no longer than needed.
Let people access, correct and delete their data, and object.
Keep the personal data secure (access control, encryption, logging).
If you use the data for your own purposes, such as training or improving the model, you are a controller for that and need your own lawful basis and notice.
Have a data processing agreement with every AI vendor that handles the personal data for you.
If the data leaves the EEA (e.g. a US model API), use a transfer tool such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or SCCs.
When you run the system on a customer's personal data, act only on their documented instructions under a data processing agreement.
Get the customer's approval for sub-processors (e.g. your model API) and flow the same terms down.
Help the customer with data subject requests, breaches and DPIAs, and delete or return the data at the end.
